                                           THE RB-47 UFO CASE -- A NEW EXPLANATION

                                                        By   Philip J. Klass


                 This is an analysis of one of the most curious uro         on record . It illust :-'1\::...!S
            that a UFO report \·:hich may at first seem to be explainable only in terms of an extr =:t-
            terrestrial spaceship can, when investigated in depth , yield a       pl ausib le, if less
            exotic, explanation.

                 The case involves an Air Force RB -47 on a fli ght ove r four southern states ( t j ssi-
            ssippi, Louisiana, Texas and Oklahoma) during the pre-da1-m hours of .J uly 17 , 1957. An
            accoun t of the incident was pub l ished in the July, 1971, i s sue of the AIAA magazine
            Astronautics & Aeronauti cs (p . 66) . It was written by the late Dr. James E. 1-lcOonald,
            an outspoken proponent of the hypothesis that the Earth is being visited by space-
            ships from other worlds .

                  NcDonald ' s i nvestigation convinced him that an "unusual craft," which had the
            ability to f ly at super sonic speed and to hover, had "played tag" with the RB-47 for
            approximately two hours. The presence of the "unusual craft," McDonald believed, t,ras
            confirmed by three independent means: visual sightings by the RB- 47 pilot and co-pilot;
            by electronic intelligence (Elint) equipment aboard the RB-47; and by an Air Defense
            Co.nmdnd ground radar located at Duncanville, Texas, near Dallas .

            t e chnological phenomena." (UFO symposium sponsored by the American Association for

            occurred more than 14 yea4s ago, is that the principals have difficulty in accurately
            rucalling some details. A more se=ious problem is possible embellishment, due to the
            passage of time and repeated re-Lelling of the story . Emb ellishment need not be t he
            resu lt of a conscious effort to alLer the facts. A principal may unconsciously report
            hoH he thinks he should have behaved at the ti me of surprise or stress, rather than
            hoh lte actuall y did behave.
